headline: Holgate's New Cut Is Holding Bass at Night — Bluefish Chew Through the Bunker at Beach Haven Inlet
subhead: A fresh cut reshaped the south end after last week's swell, and it's funneling both the bait and the bite right where I said it would.
body_markdown:
I walked the Holgate refuge line Sunday morning at low water and the beach looked different than it did two weeks ago. That swell we picked up off the back of the offshore fetch — buoy readings out at the Bight were pushing close to four feet at five seconds — did some real work down there. There's a new cut forming about three hundred yards north of the old one, a deeper trough cutting in at an angle instead of straight, with a sandbar building up on the inside edge that's holding water even on the bottom of the tide. That's the kind of structure change that gets me excited, because a new cut means new current, and new current means bait gets pushed and pinned in places it wasn't a month ago.

And sure enough, that's exactly where the bunker pods have been stacking up on the last two hours of the incoming. We flagged this last week — said the bait would keep funneling south with the tide and the blitz activity would spread down toward LBI, and that's precisely what's happening. Beach Haven Inlet and the jetty rocks at Barnegat Light have both had bluefish working through bunker schools on the tide changes, mostly the last hour of the ebb and first hour of the flood when the current squeezes bait through the throat of the inlet. These aren't the giant coastwide blitzes you're seeing up in Belmar and Sandy Hook, but they're real — cocktail blues to six pounds, occasional bigger ones mixed in, busting bait on the surface for ten, fifteen minute windows before they slide off. Poppers and metal — Ava jigs, Deadly Dicks — thrown right into the froth on the BL jetty rocks has been the play. Don't waste time false-casting. When you see the wash go white, get the lure in the water.

Stripers are the trickier story right now. Water's warm enough along this whole stretch that the bass have gone nocturnal on us, same pattern you're seeing from here up through the Sound. Daytime jigging in the inlet has been mostly a bust — I had two charters last week that worked bucktails through the Little Egg Inlet channel for three hours combined and came up with one short fish. But after dark, working bunker chunks on a fish-finder rig off the tip of Holgate, or live-lining a bunker back in the wash off Beach Haven Ridge, that's been putting bigger fish in the box. One angler I know well boated a 34-inch fish off the Ridge Tuesday night on a livelined bunker, bite came right at the top of the tide around 10:30 with almost no current running — that neap tide we're sliding into off today's first-quarter moon is softening the push through the inlet, which is actually opening up a wider bite window instead of one hard-and-fast peak. If you're going after bass right now, plan your trip around dusk through midnight rather than midday, and fish the slower water on the inside of structure where bunker schools tend to bunch up when the tide goes quiet.

Fluke are the one thing on this beat you can set your watch to right now, and that hasn't changed. Little Egg Inlet channel edges, the deeper cuts off Graveling Point, and the flats running out toward the Mullica mouth have all been holding fish on the moving water — both stages of the tide, though the last two hours of the ebb has been the more consistent producer as bait gets pulled out of Great Bay through the inlet. Four-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on quarter to half-ounce bucktails, dragged slow along the bottom in eight to fourteen feet, is still the go-to combination. A few guys working the deeper holes off Beach Haven have had fluke to five pounds on chartreuse bucktails tipped with squid strips, fished right on the channel drop where the sand gives way to mud.

Weakfish have been a quiet bright spot in the upper Mullica and around the mouth of Great Bay on calm, warm evenings — small numbers, but real fish, mostly in the 16 to 19 inch range, working soft plastics like three-inch Gulp shrimp on light jigheads right at last light when the water goes glassy. That rebuild we expected on stable, warm nights looks like it's happening, slowly. Not a bite you plan a whole trip around yet, but worth a stop if you're already out there working the tide near Graveling Point.

Kingfish are scattered but present in the surf from Ship Bottom down through Surf City, mostly on bloodworm strips fished on a high-low rig in the second and third bar troughs during the morning incoming.

Looking ahead, I'd keep an eye on that new Holgate cut — cuts like that tend to hold their shape for two to three weeks before another swell reworks them, so there's a window here. With the neap tide softening current through the end of the week, I'd focus striper efforts on the after-dark bunker bite around Beach Haven Ridge and Holgate, work the fluke on the stronger ebb tides through Little Egg Inlet, and keep bucktails and poppers rigged and ready at the jetties in case the bluefish push further south the way the bait's been moving. If the bunker keep funneling this direction through the weekend, Barnegat Light could see the blitz intensify rather than fade.
